implementation_notes: Rust's core library is the combinator library for the pattern's two canonical domains: `Option::and_then`/`or_else`/`filter`/`map` and `Result::and_then`/`or_else`/`map_err` chain fallible values as values, `Iterator::map`/`filter`/`flat_map`/`fold`/`chain` are the collection combinators, and `?` is the syntax that flattens a chain of `and_then`s (Rust By Example even titles the page 'Combinators: and_then'). Method chaining on these types replaces any class hierarchy; a trait-object structure remains justified when the DSL must be object-safe, stored heterogeneously or extended by downstream crates.
pitfalls: Iterator adaptors are lazy: a chain without a consumer does nothing, and side effects inside `map` are a smell (`inspect` exists for observation).
Long chains hide control flow; past a handful of steps, extracting a function with `?` reads better than one expression.
Ownership friction: closures that take the error by value (`or_else`) conflict with later use of that error, and mutable borrows inside adaptors rarely fit.

variants.name: nom/combine parser combinators
variants.implementation_notes: The parser specialisation ships as crates: nom parsers are functions over input returning `IResult`, composed with combinators such as `alt` (choice), `many0`/`many1` (repetition), `tag`/`take_while` (recognition) and `preceded`/`delimited` (bracketing), with a focus on zero-copy streaming input. Choose a crate when the DSL is a text or binary grammar; choose the standard library variant for `Option`/`Result`/iterator work, because a parser crate adds a dependency and its own error taxonomy.
pitfalls: Recoverable versus fatal errors (`Err::Error` vs `Err::Failure`) decide whether `alt` may try the next branch; choosing wrong makes alternatives stop trying.
A parser must consume input on success - a zero-width success inside `many0` loops forever (nom guards known empty parsers, not user-written ones).
Input lifetimes are viral: the parser's input type (`&str`, `&[u8]`, streaming) appears in every combinator signature and error type.

variants.name: futures::FutureExt adaptors over async values
variants.implementation_notes: The same algebra applies to asynchronous values: `futures::FutureExt` provides `map`, `then`, `flatten`, `fuse` and friends, while the free functions `join`/`try_join`/`select` combine several futures - and `StreamExt` mirrors the iterator adaptors for asynchronous sequences. With `async`/`await` most sequential combinators become linear code, so the adaptors are kept mainly for concurrency (run in parallel, take the first result, race with a deadline). Choose them when steps overlap in time; write plain `await` when they do not.
pitfalls: Futures are lazy: constructing a combinator chain does nothing until it is awaited or polled, so a dropped future silently skips work (including its side effects).
`join` waits for every future even when one fails, and a cancelled combinator drops the other future mid-flight, so partial work must be considered.
Async combinators are `!Send` by default: holding a non-`Send` value across an `await` breaks multi-threaded runtimes.
